chapter: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
title: Writing weekly show music for a stock company at Kansas City's Criterion
summary: At the Criterion theater the brothers wrote opening and closing choruses and songs for weekly shows starring Dodo Green.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: How about when you got to Kansas City? Uh, what was happening in Kansas City? Was there any good musicians there that you heard? Were you there long enough to hear any?

Well, yeah, my...when we went to Kansas City, my brother and I, they had a Negro show there... Oh, our job was to do nothing but write music for each...each week. See, it...they had a...you know...they had a couple of guys that wrote the story for each week, you know. Though, of course, those days, there was a lot

of producers, that if he see your show in New York, he...he'd write it all down, and when he'd get to Kansas City, he'd produce it and maybe add a little something to it, and they had...some of them had ten or twelve shows in their book, and they'd put 'em on a week, changed week at a week, and still they would be writing stuff, and then they'd buy...uh, stories from the printers, you know. They had houses...you can buy stories now from houses, and you can rewrite them, and we used to write all the music for the shows. They'd give us the plot this week and the story--they only run 'bout hour, y'know, and then they have motion pictures. And we would write an opening chorus, maybe one or two songs, a closing chorus or something, and maybe a big number in the middle where they done a lot of dancing.
Yeah. The Criterion was the name of the theater. Yeah.
And was it for the same performers every week, or was it for different performers?
Yeah. A stock company. Yeah. Yeah.
And how long did you stay in Kansas...?

Dodo Green was a big comedian in those days, and he was the star--like Bert Williams, see? He was the type of Bert Williams, y'know. Had old-fashioned Negro with the...with the slow walking and yassuh, boss, and all that...all that [inaudible] and... That was our job. All we...we didn't have to play or nothin'. We just stayed home and...course, we'd write the words and lyrics and the uh...the uh...the music for the opening chorus. You know, and the

opening chorus was generally, you know, uh, three or four choruses together, you know, of different styles and different things, they may fast chorus and then slow down to waltz, and they'd do a little something in the waltz and then back to jazz something, and then a march...something. You know. You know what opening chorus is. Then we'd write a situation song here somewhere. If there's a love scene, we'd write a love song or take one of our old songs we had that fitted and put it in there and then they always would close with a big chorus closing, and your curtain's over--your show is over. That's all we had to do. We worked there four, five months. We left there and went with Bill Bailey, I told you.
